objection.quote: Insert $c$ at its first such occurrence. Until the next occurrence nothing changes; at that next occurrence the element selected there is dispensable, because that selected set is already met by $c$. Repeating between consecutive occurrences shows that the branch has a contracted node, contrary to the pruning rule.
objection.witness: NON-SEQUITUR. Established premises: the pruned tree has an infinite branch $x_1,x_2,\ldots$ with selected sets $F_k$ disjoint from $\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}$, and some $c\in C$ lies in infinitely many $F_k$. The text then 'inserts $c$' into the branch and observes that on the MODIFIED branch a later selected element becomes dispensable. But the tree's contraction rule applies to nodes of the actual branch, whose labels never contain $c$; nothing shown implies that on the original branch an earlier chosen element becomes dispensable, so no node of the original branch is contracted and no contradiction with the pruning rule follows. Moreover 'dispensable', 'contract', and 'branches which can still be extended to an inclusion-minimal finite transversal' are never defined precisely enough for the claimed contradiction to be checkable; the inference that the pruned tree is finite is therefore unsupported.
objection.load_bearing: Finiteness of the number $s$ of minimal transversals $B_1,\ldots,B_s$ is exactly what supplies a finite modulus; the entire lemma rests on the claim that the pruned search tree is finite, and that claim is obtained only from this König-lemma paragraph.
